How did a doctor push a tube into his own heart...
and survive?
In nineteen twenty nine, doctors believed touching the inside of a heart meant death.
So when Werner Forssmann, just twenty five, asked to try it, his boss said no.
He did it anyway.
But he needed tools, and the nurse who kept them had one rule.
Try it on her first.
According to his own memoir, he strapped her to the table and numbed her arm.
Then, while she waited, he quietly cut open his own.
He slid a thin, bendy tube into a vein at his elbow.
Slowly, he pushed.
More than half a metre.
There was one problem.
He couldn't see where the tube had gone.
So, with it still inside him, he walked to the x ray room.
The picture came out.
The tip of the tube was sitting inside his heart.
And he was still alive.
He thought he'd be a hero.
Instead, a famous surgeon reportedly called it a circus stunt.
Years later, he wasn't even a heart doctor.
He treated bladders in a small town.
Then, twenty seven years after that walk to the x ray room, he won the Nobel Prize.
Today, doctors slide tubes into hearts every single day.
Because the secret was simple.
Every vein in your arm is a road that leads back to your heart.
He didn't break into his heart.
He followed the road home.
